newsitem.title: USA: Saturday talks crucial on summit arms issues.
newsitem.headline: Saturday talks crucial on summit arms issues.

text.p: A meeting in Washington this Saturday between the U.S. and Russian foreign ministers will be crucial to cutting a deal on further nuclear weapons reductions in time for next week's Helsinki summit.

Expert-level discussions in Moscow last week produced no movement either on the START II strategic arms reduction treaty and proposed follow-on START III reductions or on ballistic missile defences, senior U.S. officials acknowledge.

But the Americans believe the Russians know that resolving these disputes is important to a successful summit between President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin in the Finnish capital on March 19-20, and that, as one put it, "they (the Russians) want to make the summit a success."

Still, U.S. officials are guarded in their predictions and some outside experts tend toward pessimism, even though Yeltsin now appears physically stronger and more in politcal control after months of serious health problems.
"The U.S.-Russia arms control agenda is in serious trouble," says Jack Mendelsohn of the Arms Control Association, a private think-tank.

Mendelsohn says the summit could break the impasse, but adds that if the two leaders fail to seize the opportunity to adopt a declaration committing them to a "bold arms control package ... prospects are dim for an improved U.S.-Russian security relationship and for progress on arms control."

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is due to have a working lunch on Saturday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. He meets Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday and Clinton on Monday.

In the runup to Helsinki, much focus has been on whether Yeltsin will signal officially at the summit his intent to sign a charter defining Russia's relations with NATO by the time alliance leaders meet in July to decide on new members.
The charter is seen as a crucial mechanism tying Russia to European security decisions into the next century and calming Moscow's fears about an enlarged NATO someday turning hostile.
But the arms control issues are a critical subtext because they affect Russia's perception of its security.
"Our main (arms control) objective at the summit will be to get the Russians to move quickly to ratify START II," said one senior U.S. official referring to the pact signed in 1993.
The Russian parliament has refused to ratify START II and Yeltsin, improving after being ill for eight months, until now has not been in a position to fight on its behalf.

Communists and nationalists in the Duma argue the START II treaty took advantage of Russia at a time of weakness. The pact requires both sides to reduce their deployed warheads from about 6,000 each under the START I to no more than 3,500 each.
More importantly for Moscow, it forces Russia to eliminate entirely its huge advantage in land-based multi-warhead strategic nuclear missiles, the most destabilzing arms.

Several factors have made Russia think twice about the wisdom of START II. One is NATO expansion. Another is pressure by Congress to have the United States deploy a national ballistic missile defence system. A third is adminstration plans to deploy highly-capable theatre missile defences.
Russia, lacking the money to establish like systems, fears such defences would undermine its remaining nuclear deterrent.
These concerns are compounded by the fact that, under START II, Russia would have to spend more to build up its single-warhead missiles to stay even with the United States.

To allay Russian concerns, Washington proposed new reductions to 2,000-2,500 warheads per side and wants the two presidents to agree at the summit to begin negotiations on this START III treaty right after START II is ratified.
Also, U.S. officials said they agreed a START III treaty would require destruction, not just removal, of warheads, so the warheads cannot be refitted on missiles quickly.

Russia also sought to extend START II implementation beyond a treaty-mandated date of 2003. U.S. officials refused to amend START II because it would require new ratification by the Senate. But the extension could be included in START III.

The two sides also worked on what defensives systems will be permitted and how they affect the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. But a senior official said after last week's Moscow talks: "We're not much further along on that."
That was the first U.S. chance to explain to Russia a NATO-proposal for new cuts in conventional forces in Europe, another element in NATO's campaign to calm Moscow's fears.

Washington urged Moscow to make a counterproposal at the Conference on Disarmament in Vienna, where this deal will be negotiated among 30 countries. But U.S. officials said the two sides remain at impasse over Russia's demand for a ban on permanently stationed NATO forces on the territory of new alliance members and for an alliance cap so that the forces of new NATO members do not add to NATO force totals.
